content: The European Council Directive 93/42/EEC, dated June 14, 1993, defines a medical device as any instrument, apparatus, appliance, material, or other article, whether used alone or in combination, including software necessary for its proper application. These devices are intended by the manufacturer for use in humans for purposes such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring, treating, or alleviating diseases. They may also be used for diagnosing, monitoring, treating, alleviating, or compensating for injuries or disabilities, investigating, replacing, or modifying anatomical structures or physiological processes, or controlling conception. Importantly, these devices do not achieve their primary intended action in or on the human body through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means, although such means may assist their function. In the UK, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) oversees the regulation of medical devices under European legislation. It is critical to distinguish medical devices from medicinal products. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) defines a medical device as an instrument, apparatus, implement, machine, contrivance, implant, in vitro reagent, or other similar or related article, including component parts or accessories. These devices are recognized in the official National Formulary or the United States Pharmacopeia or their supplements. They are intended for use in diagnosing diseases or other conditions, or in curing, mitigating, treating, or preventing diseases in humans or animals. They may also be intended to affect the structure or function of the body in humans or animals. However, they do not achieve their primary intended purposes through chemical action within or on the body and are not dependent on being metabolized to achieve their primary purposes, as defined by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. 1. Class I: General Controls Class I devices pose minimal potential harm to users and are typically simpler in design compared to Class II or Class III devices. These devices are subject to general controls, which include manufacturer registration with the FDA, adherence to good manufacturing practices, proper branding and labeling, notification to the FDA before marketing, and general reporting procedures. Most Class I devices are exempt from good manufacturing practices and FDA notification regulations. Examples of Class I devices include tongue depressors, bedpans, elastic bandages, examination gloves, and handheld surgical instruments. 2. Class II: In addition to general controls, these devices are subject to special controls, which may include specific labeling requirements, mandatory performance standards, and post-market surveillance. Class II devices are held to a higher standard of assurance to confirm that they perform as intended and do not cause harm to patients or users. These devices are typically non-invasive and include items such as x-ray machines, powered wheelchairs, infusion pumps, surgical drapes, surgical needles, suture materials, and acupuncture needles. 3. Class III: These devices require premarket approval, which involves a scientific review to confirm their safety and effectiveness. Class III devices are typically life-supporting or life-sustaining, used in situations critical to preventing significant impairment of human health, or associated with a potential unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Examples of Class III devices include replacement heart valves, silicone gel-filled breast implants, implanted cerebral stimulators, implantable pacemaker pulse generators, and endosseous implants (excluding root-form endosseous dental implants, which have been reclassified as Class II). In the European Union and European Economic Area, medical devices are classified into four categories based on risk levels, as outlined in Annex IX of Directive 93/42/EEC. These categories are Class I, Class IIa, Class IIb, and Class III. However, for Class II to Class III devices, this certification must be supported by a Notified Body, an accredited testing organization that validates compliance with the European Directive. The classification of devices in the EU depends on factors such as the duration of body contact, invasiveness, use of an energy source, effects on the central circulation or nervous system, diagnostic impact, or incorporation of medicinal products. Certified medical devices must display the CE mark on their packaging, along with harmonized pictograms and ISO-standardized logos indicating essential features such as instructions for use, expiration date, manufacturer, sterility, and single-use status. Notable regulatory and certification providers for medical devices include Underwriters Laboratories. Prominent medical device companies include Abbott Laboratories, Baxter International, BD, Boston Scientific, Medtronic, Johnson & Johnson, Siemens Medical Solutions, and many others.
